title: Harun al-Rashid and the Damsel and Abu Nowas (简体中文)

full_text:
The Caliph Harun al-Rashid was sitting in his garden pavilion beside a sparkling fountain, accompanied by an intelligent and witty court maiden named Zubayr. As the breeze ruffled the rosebushes, the Caliph resolved to test the famous court poet Abu Nowas, whose audacious humor was both the delight and exasperation of the court.

The Caliph challenged Zubayr to pose an impossible poetic riddle: 'When Abu Nowas enters, I shall recite the first half of an improbable verse; you shall recite the second; and if he cannot complete it on the spot with rhyme, meter, and brilliant wit, he shall pay twenty dinars to the gardeners!'

Presently, Abu Nowas entered the pavilion, bowing low with his usual whimsical grin.

The Caliph immediately cleared his throat and recited:
'The lion in his den bowed down before the mouse,'

Zubayr quickly added with a playful smile:
'And begged for mercy meekly outside his little house!'

Abu Nowas did not pause for the blink of an eye. Adjusting his embroidered turban, he declaimed with thunderous gravity:
'For though the lion's claw can tear the oak in twain,
A thorn within his paw was pulled by love again;
Thus power learns to kneel where gentle deeds abide,
And wisdom cures the hurt that steel could never hide!'

The Caliph and Zubayr stared in astonishment at how effortlessly the poet had turned their silly rhyme into a profound philosophical allegory.

Harun al-Rashid burst into hearty laughter, tossed a purse of fifty gold dinars into Abu Nowas’s hands, and exclaimed: 'By my ancestors, Abu Nowas, your tongue is quicker than an arrow in flight! Even when we set a snare for your wits, you weave our cords into a carpet of gold!'
moral: Spontaneous wit and poetic eloquence can defuse imperial wrath and bring laughter to solemn halls. [ZH]
